prompt: Which role on a service account lets its holder create a machine that runs as the account?

choices.text: `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator`
choices.why: That one is for impersonation: asking for a token in the account's name.

choices.text: `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser`
choices.why: Right. It allows attaching the account to what its holder creates.

choices.text: `roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin`
choices.why: Admin creates and manages accounts; attaching one is the user role's job.

choices.text: `roles/compute.viewer`
choices.why: A viewer creates nothing, machines included.

prompt: A developer has no role on `planner-prod`, but holds `serviceAccountUser` on a production service account that holds Editor there. What can the developer do in production?
hint: Acting as the account is holding its roles.

choices.text: Nothing, because the developer holds no role on the project
choices.why: The account's roles are the developer's, in effect, through the attach.

choices.text: Read the account's settings and nothing more
choices.why: `serviceAccountUser` is far more than read: it is acting as the account.

choices.text: Grant Editor to others
choices.why: Editor cannot grant roles; that is Owner's addition.

choices.text: Whatever Editor allows
choices.why: Right. This is the commonest way a narrow IAM design leaks.

prompt: Why should `serviceAccountUser` be granted on one service account rather than on the project?
hint: On the project it reaches every account in it.

choices.text: It would cover every account in the project
choices.why: Right. Somebody deploying one function could run as any account, Editor-holding defaults included.

choices.text: It cannot be granted on a project
choices.why: It can, and that is the problem the question is about.

choices.text: A project-wide grant expires after a day
choices.why: Grants do not expire unless a condition says so.

choices.text: Accounts ignore grants made on the project
choices.why: They honour them, inherited like any other grant.

prompt: Code on a machine with an attached service account calls Pub/Sub. Where does its token come from?
hint: An address only the machine can reach.

choices.text: A key file installed with the machine
choices.why: No key is involved with an attached account.

choices.text: The developer's own credentials, copied in
choices.why: The machine runs as the account, not as a person.

choices.text: The metadata server, at `169.254.169.254`
choices.why: Right. It hands out a token of about an hour, renewed on demand, and no key exists.

choices.text: The emulator, which issues tokens
choices.why: The emulator issues nothing; it ignores tokens altogether.

prompt: Which Google API does impersonation call to get a token in a service account's name?
hint: The refusal in the lab named it.

choices.text: Pub/Sub, which accepts any service account
choices.why: The Pub/Sub call never happened: the token request came first and was refused.

choices.text: The Resource Manager, `getProject`
choices.why: That reads a project. Tokens come from IAM Credentials.

choices.text: IAM Credentials, `generateAccessToken`
choices.why: Right. `iamcredentials.googleapis.com` is the whole of impersonation.

choices.text: The metadata server on the laptop
choices.why: A laptop has no metadata server; that is a Google Cloud machine's.

prompt: In the lab, `gcloud pubsub topics list --impersonate-service-account=...` was refused, though Pub/Sub points at the emulator. Why did it reach Google at all?
hint: What does gcloud need before the Pub/Sub call?

choices.text: It asks Google for the borrowed token first
choices.why: Right. Only IAM Credentials can mint the token, and no emulator answers it.

choices.text: The override was removed by the flag
choices.why: The override stays. It just was never used, because the token came first.

choices.text: The emulator forwards impersonated calls to Google
choices.why: The emulator forwards nothing; the request never reached it.

choices.text: Impersonation is only allowed against real APIs
choices.why: No such rule. The token simply has to come from Google.

prompt: By default, at most how many seconds does an impersonated token last?
A token from impersonation is pasted by mistake into a public chat. Why is that less serious than pasting a key?

choices.text: Tokens grant no roles, only identity
choices.why: A token carries every role of the account while it lasts.

choices.text: Google rejects tokens used from a second address
choices.why: No such check exists. The expiry is what limits the damage.

choices.text: A token reaches only the emulator
choices.why: A real token works against Google's real APIs.

choices.text: It expires within the hour
choices.why: Right. A key works until somebody deletes it; a token stops on its own.

prompt: `deployer.tf` grants `serviceAccountTokenCreator` with `google_service_account_iam_member` rather than on the project. What does that limit?
hint: On what resource is the grant?

choices.text: The deployer may act only during on-call hours
choices.why: Nothing in the grant mentions time; a condition would.

choices.text: The on-call group may borrow the deployer and no other account
choices.why: Right. The grant sits on one account, which is the rule from the first section.

choices.text: The group may create keys for the deployer
choices.why: Token Creator mints short-lived tokens, not keys.

choices.text: The deployer may impersonate the group
choices.why: A group cannot be impersonated. The arrow points the other way.

prompt: Why is the deployer's `email` known in the plan, before anything is created?

choices.text: It is built from the account id and the project id
choices.why: Right. `deployer@planner-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com` follows from both.

choices.text: The provider asked Google for it
choices.why: A plan asked Google nothing.

choices.text: Google reserves emails a day in advance
choices.why: No reservation is involved; the address follows from names you chose.

choices.text: Every service account shares one email
choices.why: Each account has its own, which is what makes it a principal.

prompt: Match each way of proving you are a service account to how long its credential works.
hint: One has no end at all.

pairs.right: an hour, or up to twelve

prompt: A key for a service account has leaked. What is the first thing to do?
hint: Every copy works until one thing happens.

choices.text: Read the audit logs to see what it did
choices.why: That comes second. Until the key is deleted, it keeps working for whoever has it.

choices.text: Rotate the account's password
choices.why: A service account has no password.

choices.text: Delete the key
choices.why: Right. Deleting it ends every copy at once, and the logs are still there afterwards.

choices.text: Remove the repository the key was found in
choices.why: Copies may already exist elsewhere. Only deleting the key stops them.

prompt: A GitHub Actions workflow deploys to Google Cloud. Which credential does the lesson recommend instead of a key in a CI variable?
hint: The job already carries a signed token from GitHub.

choices.text: A key with an expiry of a year
choices.why: Still a key, and a year is a long time for a copy to work.

choices.text: Workload Identity Federation, lesson 9
choices.why: Right. The outside token is traded for a Google one, with no key at all.

choices.text: An attached account on the GitHub runner
choices.why: Attaching works for machines inside Google Cloud; a GitHub runner is outside.

choices.text: The developer's own credentials, stored as a secret
choices.why: That trades one long-lived secret for a worse one, a person's.

prompt: A third-party appliance accepts only a key file. Which control makes rotation stop being optional?
hint: A policy can give keys a lifetime.

choices.text: A reminder in the team's calendar
choices.why: A reminder is exactly the optional the question wants to avoid.

choices.text: Granting the appliance Owner, so it can rotate its own key
choices.why: That makes the appliance able to do anything, and rotates nothing.

choices.text: Storing the key in the repository next to the code
choices.why: That is how keys leak. It forces no rotation.

choices.text: `iam.serviceAccountKeyExpiryHours`, which makes keys stop working
choices.why: Right. A key that expires has to be replaced, so rotation happens.

prompt: Put the steps of rotating an unavoidable key in order.
hint: The old key goes last, and only after a check.
items: deploy it where the old one was used
confirm the old key is no longer used
trap: Deleting the old key before confirming nothing uses it is the slip: the appliance stops on the spot, and the outage is the rotation's.

prompt: A data engineer runs a nightly script on their laptop as `reports@planner-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com`, using a key file in their home directory. What should replace the key?
hint: A person running something as an account.

choices.text: A second key, so the first can be rotated
choices.why: Two keys are two leaks waiting. The person can impersonate instead.

choices.text: Editor for the engineer on the project
choices.why: That gives the person far more than the script needs, and the account is no longer used.

choices.text: An attached account on the laptop
choices.why: A laptop is outside Google Cloud and has no metadata server.

choices.text: Impersonation: Token Creator on `reports` for the engineer
choices.why: Right. The engineer signs in as themselves and borrows the account for an hour each night.
